items.title: Bloomberg reports investigators found hackers reached the propulsion system of the US-bound crude tanker VL Prosperity — the FBI says nothing was disrupted, and no attacker has been named
items.content_text: On 2 October Bloomberg reported that FBI and Coast Guard investigators found evidence that hackers accessed the propulsion system of the crude supertanker VL Prosperity as it approached the Texas coast this summer, through what it describes as outsiders gaining temporary access to the ship’s digital systems. The report rests on US officials familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified; neither agency has confirmed the finding on the record, and the Coast Guard declined to comment. Bloomberg says it was not clear how long the intruders had access or what they could have controlled, and that officials are still examining how the breach happened and who was responsible. The FBI’s on-record position is unchanged: it has no reports of operational disruption, vessel instability, danger to crews or environmental harm. What is confirmed dates from September. A joint Coast Guard and FBI statement, reported on 16 September, said cyber teams boarded two foreign-flagged, US-bound energy tankers in August “following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised”; the Coast Guard told The Record the networks were compromised by foreign cyber actors, and Rear Adm. Amy Grable, commander of Coast Guard Cyber Command, told CBS News that investigators found malicious cyber activity aboard the first vessel. Per Dragos, VL Prosperity was boarded on 21 August in the Atlantic and the second tanker on 24 August in the Gulf of Mexico, where Bloomberg also places it. The agencies have not named the second ship and published names for it conflict, so this page does not name it. VL Prosperity is a 333-metre Liberian-flagged crude supertanker that loaded at Sidi Kerir, Egypt, for Galveston; its manager, HMM Ocean Service, said in September that it had been cleared for normal operations. The new report narrows the gap between a compromised network and machinery control, but it does not say the intruders operated anything: in September CISA told Bloomberg the actors did not appear to have taken control of the vessels themselves, and earlier claims of altered engine speed, cooling and fuel systems still trace only to Iran’s Mehr News Agency and remain unverified. Bloomberg’s figure of nearly 20 vessels tracked for cyber threats by September was already public and is not a new finding. No agency has linked the Vivit Africa LNG case, where the crew’s claims remain unverified and the Italian Coast Guard recorded a malfunction (see Incidents), and Texas Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian cited the boardings on 24 September (see Regulation & Policy). No new official statement had appeared by 6 October. For oil and gas operators the point is the interface rather than the ship: crude and LPG cargoes bound for US Gulf Coast terminals, a reported intrusion that reached propulsion, and a federal cyber response that reached the berth.

items.title: The Vivit Africa LNG crew’s claim that attackers took control of safety-valve, tank-pressure and boil-off systems is still unverified — the Italian Coast Guard records a cargo-monitoring malfunction of undetermined cause
items.content_text: Bloomberg first reported on 18 September that the crew lost access to some internal control systems in early September as the ship approached the Adriatic. On 21 September Splash247 published the account the crew of Vivit Africa LNG sent to the outlet and, it says, to Korean Register, the ship’s class society. The crew claims that attackers gained temporary control of the steam-pressure and safety-valve systems while the ship transited the Strait of Gibraltar, and later, in the Adriatic, of tank-pressure control, pressure-relief valves and boil-off gas management — which they say significantly increased the risk of tank rupture and explosion. Splash247 states plainly that it has not independently verified the claims, and no other party has confirmed them. The official record is narrower. Italian Coast Guard Capt. Roberto D’Arrigo says the master reported “a malfunction in the systems used to monitor cargo parameters” that required company technicians, that the cause “could not be identified”, and that the Coast Guard issued a navigational warning and intervened only for safety of navigation. Kongsberg Maritime, which supplies equipment aboard, said on 18 September it was too early to draw conclusions about the cause or any security implications; Vitol, the charterer, declined to comment beyond confirming the charter, and H-Line Shipping, the owner, and Korean Register have not responded. What is confirmed is the movement: the vessel loaded at Cameron LNG in Louisiana for the Adriatic LNG terminal near Rovigo, idled off Italy without discharging, then abandoned the call and sailed west toward Algeciras. Bloomberg counts it as the third tanker in about a month after the two US-bound vessels boarded by the Coast Guard and FBI, but no agency has linked the cases. Until an investigator, the class society or the equipment supplier reports, this remains a suspected incident with an unverified crew claim attached — and it is scored that way; with nothing new by 6 October, this edition rates it Medium rather than High. For oil and gas the relevance is unchanged: a US LNG export cargo, and the cargo-monitoring and tank-pressure functions that are the shipboard counterpart of terminal custody-transfer, loading and ESD data.

items.title: CenterPoint Energy confirms customer data was taken through an external-facing system — gas and electric delivery not affected
items.content_text: CenterPoint Energy, the Houston-based electric and natural gas utility, said in an SEC filing that an unauthorised third party obtained personal information on “a portion of the Company’s customers through one of the Company’s external-facing systems.” BleepingComputer reports the system was a public API with no rate limiting, web application firewall or automated access controls. Exposed data includes names, phone numbers, service and billing addresses, account numbers, billing amounts and partial Social Security numbers. An actor using the alias “4d722e4d656f77” claims to have taken 7.49 million records and has leaked data; CenterPoint has not given a count, and class-action filings allege the intrusion ran from 17 August to 1 September. The company says electric and natural gas services were not affected, and it has notified law enforcement and regulators. This is an IT and customer-data incident, not an OT one, and it is scored that way. It belongs on an oil and gas page because gas distribution utilities run exactly this kind of customer-facing API alongside SCADA for pressure and flow — and the useful question is how much those two estates share.

items.title: Symantec: the China-nexus group behind Warlock ransomware broke into a water utility and a telecom operator through on-premises SharePoint — no OT impact is described, and no energy victim is named
items.content_text: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team reported on 1 October that a group it calls Longlegs, which it describes as a China-nexus threat actor also tracked as Storm-2603, has attacked at least four organisations in the past two months: two critical infrastructure operators — a water utility and a telecommunications provider — plus a regional government body and a university, in Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries in Europe, Africa and Latin America. No victim or country is named. Symantec says the group typically gets in by exploiting several vulnerabilities in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint Server; the CVEs it names are the 2025 ToolShell flaws (CVE-2025-49704, CVE-2025-49706, CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771), alongside unspecified related SharePoint flaws. Once inside, the group steals ASP.NET machine keys, sideloads DLLs, uses Visual Studio Code tunnels and NetExec, and loads a vulnerable signed driver (CVE-2025-1055 in K7RKScan) to switch off security tools; in one intrusion Symantec documents, Warlock was pushed to at least 33 hosts through SYSVOL. Symantec does not describe any operational or OT impact at the water utility and does not say ransomware was deployed there. It is on this page as cross-sector context, not an oil and gas incident: the targets are critical infrastructure operators, the entry point is the kind of on-premises collaboration server that engineering and document-control teams often run, and machine-key theft means a server patched after compromise can still be reopened.

items.title: Recorded Future: Russia’s hybrid pressure on Europe is “largely opportunistic” for now — and a drone intercepted near Romania’s Neptun Deep offshore gas field is among its cases
items.content_text: Recorded Future’s Insikt Group published an assessment on 24 September that Russia has escalated what it calls “New Generation Warfare” tactics in Europe since February 2022, combining sabotage, drones, cyber operations and disinformation. It judges current activity “largely opportunistic”, but likely to escalate over the next two years, potentially culminating in a full-scale campaign. The incidents it cites include an explosive maritime drone intercepted near Romania’s Neptun Deep offshore gas field on 20 August 2026, a sabotage plot using military-grade explosives against cargo infrastructure at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August, DDoS and access operations against the Norwegian public sector on 30 August, and subsea cables as a growing target. Dark Reading’s coverage adds that the research cites water and wastewater targeting in Norway and Poland and attacks on Poland’s energy infrastructure in early 2026. Insikt’s recommendations include contractor and insider vetting, perimeter detection and anti-drone measures, alternative supply routes, coordination with national CERTs and phishing-resistant MFA. This is an analytic assessment attributed to Russia at assessment level; the blog names no specific unit and reports no new OT process impact. It is separate from the ENISA threat landscape below. For operators with European offshore, pipeline and terminal assets the relevance is direct: the physical and cyber threats are being assessed together, so the security planning for those assets should be too.

items.title: Microsoft profiles Storm-2570, a ransomware affiliate that switches between Qilin, DragonForce, Anubis and BERT while its tradecraft stays the same — energy and chemicals are on its victim list
items.content_text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence published a profile on 24 September of Storm-2570, a ransomware affiliate it has tracked since April 2025 that has deployed Qilin, DragonForce, Anubis and BERT ransomware. Microsoft lists victims in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Spain, the Netherlands and Puerto Rico, in sectors that include energy, chemicals, critical manufacturing and transportation as well as healthcare, education, government and financial services. It says the method of initial access “remains unconfirmed”. The tooling is mostly legitimate software: remote-management agents including Atera, MeshAgent, ScreenConnect, Splashtop and NinjaRMM; PsExec, Impacket and NetExec for lateral movement; Mimikatz, LaZagne and ntdsutil for credentials; ngrok and Cloudflare tunnels; and Rclone and s5cmd for exfiltration. Microsoft names no individual victim and describes no OT impact. Two points carry over to oil and gas. Switching ransomware brands changes the leak site, not the behaviour, so detections built on behaviour — a new RMM agent, PsExec from an unusual host, an ntdsutil run — keep working when the brand changes. And the same RMM tools are common in vendor support for plant, pipeline and terminal systems, which makes an allow-list of approved remote tools an OT control as well as an IT one.

items.title: Forescout: only 13% of network segments with OT devices are OT-only — and oil and gas is among the three sectors with the largest average “blast radius”
items.content_text: Forescout Vedere Labs published an analysis on 22 September of 47,700 network segments containing more than 2.5 million devices at 209 organisations. Its headline finding: “Of all segments containing OT devices, 13% are OT-only”; the other 87% also hold other types of device. Forescout measures “blast radius” as the number of devices that share a segment, which is roughly how far an attacker can reach from one compromised device without crossing a control. Forescout names business and professional services, healthcare, and oil and gas as the sectors with “the largest average ‘blast radius’”, while utilities, financial services and retail have the lowest; Industrial Cyber’s report of the study puts the oil and gas average at 72 devices per segment. Its recommendations are continuous asset visibility, identifying and prioritising “device convergence zones”, separating critical operational assets from enterprise IT, reducing oversized segments, policy-based access control between segments, and monitoring for segmentation drift. This is exposure data from one vendor’s dataset, not an incident, and it does not name organisations. It does describe the condition that turns an exploited edge device, like those in this edition’s KEV cards, into an OT problem.

items.title: The US puts up to $10 million on the IRGC cyber commander said to direct CyberAv3ngers — energy is on the named target list
items.content_text: On 4 September the US State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme offered up to $10 million for information on Amir Yaryab, described as a senior official of Iran’s IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command (IRGC-CEC) who leads its Cyber Operations Command. The State Department says he directs IRGC-CEC components and affiliated groups including CyberAv3ngers, Dadeh Afzar Arman and Mehrsam Andisheh Saz Nik, and that these groups have targeted critical infrastructure in the United States, Europe and the Middle East, energy and telecommunications among them. Analysis published by Security Boulevard on 9 September also names the Shahid Hemmat and Shahid Shushtari components, and ties Iran-linked groups to attacks on municipal water systems in at least 12 US states this year. The technical background is the joint CISA and FBI warning updated on 22–23 July, which said Iran-affiliated actors attacking PLCs in water and energy had widened their target set beyond Rockwell/Allen-Bradley to Schneider Modicon M340/BMX P34 and Siemens S7-1200 controllers. Those are the controller families found in wellsite automation, compressor stations, tank farms and terminal loading systems. The reward is a policy step, not a new intrusion, and the attributions are US government assessments.

items.title: Red Heron broke into self-hosted Gitea and walked out with SCADA and HMI source code from an industrial automation vendor
items.content_text: Acronis’ Threat Research Unit published findings on 13 September, reported on 14–15 September, on a campaign it attributes with moderate confidence to Red Heron, a Chinese-speaking, PRC-linked actor, exploiting CVE-2026-60004, the CVSS 9.8 Gitea remote code execution flaw fixed in Gitea 1.27.1 on 27 July. Acronis confirms 11 compromised targets across Canada, Argentina, Taiwan, the United States and Sri Lanka, including a Canadian renewable energy company, a Taiwanese industrial automation firm, municipal platforms and defence, aerospace and telecoms organisations. From the automation firm the attackers took the source code of a SCADA/HMI tool used in industrial control environments, along with IoT integrations and a network sniffer; “hundreds of repositories” were exfiltrated from a single target. The tooling includes the JITTERLY implant, with more than 30 post-exploitation commands, and a previously undocumented Linux rootkit Acronis calls SIXZUT. No oil or gas victim has been reported. The relevance is twofold: stolen HMI source gives an attacker a head start on finding flaws in products that end up in process plants, and O&G engineering teams and integrators increasingly keep PLC logic, HMI projects and SIS configuration in exactly this kind of self-hosted Git server.

items.title: NCC Group counts 1,073 ransomware attacks in August, a 2026 high, with the industrial sector bearing 31% — and energy incidents are still landing on IT, which is where the outage comes from
items.content_text: NCC Group’s review of August 2026, reported by Industrial Cyber on 28 September, counts 1,073 ransomware attacks, up 12 percent from 960 in July. The industrial sector accounted for 329 of them, about 31 percent, and North America for 473, about 44 percent. Qilin led with 164 claimed attacks, overtaking The Gentlemen. NCC also describes Aurora, a ransomware-as-a-service group active since late April that goes after manufacturing, legal, research and transportation organisations through weak or unauthenticated VPN access before encrypting hypervisors. A different tracker, Comparitech, reported on 14 September a record 997 attacks for the same month; the counts differ because each tracker has its own method, and both rest largely on leak-site claims, so a claimed victim is not a confirmed one, and neither breaks out oil and gas. The pattern they fit is the one the sector already knows from Colonial Pipeline onward — encryption lands on business systems, and operations stop because scheduling, billing, custody-transfer accounting or terminal ticketing depends on them, not because anything touched a controller.

items.title: Nozomi chains 12 flaws in the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 to root on an OT edge device — patched, and not exploited
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research on 18 September: twelve vulnerabilities in total, nine in the device firmware and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client. Firmware below V4.0 HF0 and Edge Client releases through V2.1 are affected, and Siemens has published an advisory with fixes in V4.0 HF0 and later. Nozomi demonstrated that several of the flaws can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which would allow manipulation of telemetry, suppression of alarms, access to operational data, disruption of edge services and lateral movement into the networks the device sits between. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. Two dates are worth keeping apart: CISA updated the long-standing advisory ICSA-25-135-18 on 15 September to add the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and the vendor fixes — an advisory update, not a new vulnerability — and this 18 September publication is the research behind it. The CVE identifiers in this set carry 2025 prefixes despite the 2026 disclosure, which is consistent with how the line was assigned but worth confirming against Siemens’ own advisory before you put them in a ticket. Our sector read: local processing engines and SINEMA remote access are used for edge processing and vendor connectivity at remote and unmanned sites, which is where root on an edge box buys the most.

items.title: ENISA’s 2026 Threat Landscape: 60% of unauthorised access came through known vulnerabilities, and 73% of victims were NIS2 essential or important entities
items.content_text: ENISA published its Threat Landscape 2026 on 23 September, covering calendar year 2025. As reported by Industrial Cyber, it counts 4,709 hacktivist campaigns against EU member states, more than 89% of them DDoS. It finds that 60% of unauthorised-access incidents used known vulnerabilities and that 73% of victims were classed as essential or important entities under EU rules. It records more than 48,000 new vulnerabilities, 22% more than the year before. Of state-nexus activity, 47.6% was Russia-nexus and 15.5% China-nexus. The coverage reviewed gives no energy or oil and gas breakdown, so no sector-specific figure is quoted here. Two points still apply to EU oil and gas operators, most of whom are NIS2 entities. The main way in is still a known, unpatched flaw, which is the same pattern as this edition’s KEV cards. And hacktivist activity against the EU is overwhelmingly DDoS, which argues for keeping public-facing and OT-dependent services apart.

items.title: Citrix confirms the exploited NetScaler zero-days and patches a third — CVE-2026-88771 and -88772 in KEV since 27 September, a SAML crash flaw added 4 October with a 7 October deadline, and patching does not evict an intruder
items.content_text: Citrix bulletin CTX697096 of 27 September fixed eight NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway flaws, two of them exploited. CVE-2026-88771 is an improper input validation flaw that allows unauthenticated arbitrary command execution, CVSS v4 9.5, and affects all deployments including the default configuration. CVE-2026-88772 is a memory overflow that can lead to code execution or denial of service, CVSS v4 9.5, and needs DTLS enabled, which VPN virtual servers have by default. Fixed builds are 14.1-73.37 and 13.1-64.23 and later. CISA added both to KEV the same day with a 30 September deadline, said threat actors are exploiting them globally and advised preserving forensic evidence before patching; the Dutch NCSC said exploitation had been identified at multiple Citrix customers worldwide. Google Threat Intelligence and LevelBlue describe what intruders leave behind: a PHP web shell (WHIPSHOT), a Python tunneller (SLAPSHOT), a rogue superuser account named sec_monitor, theft of the appliance configuration archive and tampered logs. Mandiant’s chief technology officer said upgrading alone will not remove post-exploitation access or address stolen credentials, and described the actors as advanced and suspected state-sponsored; no group has been named. Victim counts come from different trackers and should not be merged: Mandiant says dozens of organisations in government, education, technology, financial services, telecoms and professional services across North America and Europe; Arctic Wolf at least 78; Kevin Beaumont’s own tracking more than 100 (29 September). In the Netherlands a ministry and hospitals took Citrix environments offline as a precaution; those were shutdowns, not confirmed compromises. The third flaw, CVE-2026-88779, is a memory overflow on appliances configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider, CVSS v4 8.7. Citrix patched it on 3 October (14.1-73.41 and 13.1-64.28 and later), says it has observed targeted attacks that can lead to denial of service, and has identified no impact on the integrity of customer data; CISA added it to KEV on 4 October, due 7 October. watchTowr reproduced it as a crash-only bug and suspects it is used to knock appliances over to speed exploitation of CVE-2026-88771; one researcher reported signs of code execution on a patched honeypot, but watchTowr and Citrix describe a crash. No oil and gas victim has been named. The sector read is ours: NetScaler Gateway is a common front door for vendor and engineer remote access into refinery, gas-plant and pipeline OT DMZs, and access gained before a patch survives the patch.

items.title: CISA: ten flaws, led by a CVSS 10.0 file-exposure bug, in Toptech TMS7 and TopHAT, terminal management software for midstream fuel terminals — fixed in 7.8, not exploited
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-272-02 on 29 September for Toptech Systems TMS7 and TopHAT version 7.6.3. It lists ten vulnerabilities. The most serious, CVE-2026-71379, leaves files or directories accessible to external parties and is scored CVSS v3.1 10.0 (v4 10.0). CVE-2026-70356 allows unrestricted upload of a dangerous file type (v3.1 9.1), and five SQL injection flaws — CVE-2026-72510, CVE-2026-63713, CVE-2026-68954, CVE-2026-68068 and CVE-2026-72507 — score v3.1 9.0. The rest are a session fixation flaw (v3.1 7.1) and two low-scoring eval-injection and cross-site scripting issues. CISA says successful exploitation could let an attacker access critical data or execute arbitrary code, lists the Energy, Chemical and Transportation Systems sectors, and says the products are deployed worldwide. The fix is release 7.8, which Toptech issued on 20 July with a customer advisory, so sites still on 7.6.3 have had a fix available for more than two months. No known public exploitation has been reported to CISA, and none of the flaws is in KEV. This one is squarely in the sector: Toptech, part of IDEX, describes itself as providing batch controller hardware and terminal management solutions for the midstream oil and gas industry, and TMS7 is part of its terminal management line. In a fuel or bulk-liquid terminal, software of this class typically authorises drivers and carriers, allocates product, produces bills of lading, keeps inventory and talks to the batch controllers at the loading rack (that description is ours, not CISA’s). A database or file-system compromise there is a commercial and operational problem even if no controller is touched.

items.title: An exploited FortiMail flaw lets an unauthenticated attacker write files on the mail gateway — in KEV since 1 October, and Fortinet’s 5 October update lists fixed releases
items.content_text: Fortinet published FG-IR-26-175 on 1 October for CVE-2026-104286, a path traversal flaw combined with improper NULL-byte handling in FortiMail. Fortinet says it lets an unauthenticated attacker “write arbitrary files on the underlying system via crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests”, scores it CVSS 9.8 and says it has been reported exploited in the wild; Fortinet found the flaw internally. CISA added it to KEV the same day with a 4 October federal deadline. Affected branches are 7.2.0 to 7.2.9, 7.4.0 to 7.4.8, 7.6.0 to 7.6.6 and 8.0.0 to 8.0.1. When the advisory first appeared the fixed releases were listed as planned, with no date. Fortinet’s 5 October update now lists 7.4.9, 7.6.7 and 8.0.2 or later, and tells 7.2 users to move to the 7.4 branch or above. Its workarounds still matter until each unit is upgraded: disable Identity-Based Encryption (IBE), restrict webmail access from untrusted networks, and use web application firewall rules to block path-traversal requests to the IBE endpoint. No actor, campaign or victim has been disclosed. The sector read is ours: a mail gateway is not OT, but in oil and gas it is the relay for vendor advisories, nominations and scheduling, and the alarm and production-report email that leaves plant networks, and a file-write foothold on it is a trusted position next to the systems the business side of operations depends on.

items.title: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager: an exploited authentication bypass gives unauthenticated attackers admin-level API access to the system that configures every site — CVSS 9.8, in KEV since 30 September
items.content_text: Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-76504 on 30 September. Improper handling of URI encoding in Catalyst SD-WAN Manager lets a remote, unauthenticated request get past an authentication rule meant to restrict a specific API endpoint, giving administrator-level access. Cisco scores it CVSS 9.8, says there are no workarounds, and states that its PSIRT “became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability” in September 2026. CISA added it to KEV on 30 September with a 3 October deadline, and Cisco revised the advisory to version 1.1 on 2 October. Fixed releases are 20.9.10.1, 20.12.8.2, 20.15.6.1, 20.18.4.1, 26.1.2.1 and 26.2.1; releases older than 20.9 must migrate to a fixed release. BleepingComputer counts it as the fifth exploited Catalyst SD-WAN zero-day of 2026. No actor or victim has been named. The sector read is ours: where SD-WAN carries traffic between control centres, compressor and pump stations, terminals and field offices, the manager is the system that pushes configuration and policy to every edge router, so admin access to it is a route to changing segmentation at every site at once. It is the same exposure as the exploited Arista VeloCloud orchestrator in KEV since 22 September (see Arista VeloCloud).

items.title: MikroTik RouterOS: the exploited “MikroTrick” chain is fully in KEV, and CISA now flags a separate pre-authentication CVSS 9.8 web-management flaw that is not — the routers at remote sites
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-67279 in MikroTik RouterOS to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 25 September, with a federal remediation deadline of 28 September. It is an SSH workflow flaw that, in the KEV entry’s words, “could allow an unauthenticated client to open a session channel and send an exec request”, and that can be chained for unauthenticated exploitation of CVE-2026-86060; reporting gives it CVSS 6.9 without stating the version. It joins CVE-2026-86060, an argument-injection flaw, and CVE-2026-67277, a missing-authentication flaw in the bandwidth-test service, both added to KEV on 10 September. CERT Polska reported on 5 September that a two-flaw SSH chain it calls “MikroTrick” has been exploited in the wild since about 2 September. Its 22 September technical analysis names the chain: CVE-2026-67279 combined with CVE-2026-86060, which gives an unauthenticated attacker full administrative control. CVE-2026-67276, which an earlier edition of this card placed in the chain, is not in KEV. CERT Polska lists RouterOS 7.24.2, 7.23.4 and 6.49.21 as fixed; a related flaw, CVE-2026-67278, needs 7.24.3 or 7.23.6 because the earlier fix was incomplete. Separately, CISA’s ICS advisory ICSA-26-272-06 of 29 September covers CVE-2026-84411, a pre-authentication integer underflow in RouterOS web management that can lead to code execution or denial of service, scored CVSS v3.1 9.8 and fixed in RouterOS 7.24 and later; no exploitation has been reported and it is not in KEV. Shadowserver counted more than 122,500 MikroTik devices with SSH reachable from the internet in early September — an exposure count, not a count of compromised or unpatched devices. No victims or sectors have been named, so there is no confirmed oil and gas victim. The sector read is ours: inexpensive, capable routers are a common contractor choice for cellular and fixed-wireless backhaul at wellpads, tank batteries, remote valve and meter stations and pipeline block-valve sites — often the one device on site with a route to both the SCADA host and the internet.

items.title: Lantronix G520 cellular gateways do not properly verify software signatures — CISA says an attacker could replace the software and run code as root; fixed in 2.6.0.7R6
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-272-01 on 29 September for the Lantronix G520 Series cellular gateway, version 2.6.0.4R6_stable. CVE-2026-91191 is an improper verification of a cryptographic signature and CVE-2026-84409 is a cross-site scripting flaw; each is scored CVSS v3.1 7.5 (v4 7.7). CISA says successful exploitation could allow an attacker to “replace software and execute arbitrary code with root privileges”. It lists the Energy, Water and Wastewater, and Transportation Systems sectors, with deployment worldwide. Lantronix release 2.6.0.7R6 fixes both. No known public exploitation has been reported to CISA, and neither flaw is in KEV. The sector read is ours: industrial cellular gateways like this are how many wellpads, tank batteries, meter stations and cathodic-protection sites get RTU and flow-computer data back to SCADA, and a gateway that will accept replaced software is a root foothold on the one device that bridges the site to the carrier network. It is the same remote-site edge question as the exploited MikroTik routers above, without the exploitation.

items.title: Arista’s VeloCloud SD-WAN orchestrator, a CVSS 10 flaw, is being exploited — the system that pushes configuration to your remote sites. F5 BIG-IP APM joins it in KEV
items.content_text: Arista Security Advisory 0183 (22 September) covers CVE-2026-93952 in the on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO), CVSS v3.1 10.0. Improper input validation lets an attacker reach privileged internal VCO functions without VCO tenant or operator credentials. Arista says it is “known to be actively exploited”. The flaw is exposed where certificate-based Edge-to-VCO authentication is configured. Hosted VCO is already patched. Fixes are 5.2.3.16 or later and 6.4.2.8 or later; Arista lists no fix yet for the 6.1.x and 7.0.x trains. Its indicators include files named .vcnode.js and vc-sysmond, an x-vc-opt HTTP header and source addresses 142.93.149.77 and 104.248.126.159. Its interim advice is to restrict the VCO web interface to trusted networks. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 22 September alongside F5 BIG-IP APM CVE-2026-94127, CVSS v3.1 9.8 (v4.0 9.3). That is an unauthenticated heap overflow, exploitable only where a virtual server carries both an APM access policy and an OAuth authorization-server profile; F5 advisory K000162605 lists engineering hotfixes, and CISA’s KEV entry advises applying F5’s iRule first to allow forensic triage, then patching. Both were due 25 September, and the two Check Point flaws in the same batch have their own cards. SD-WAN is a common way to connect compressor and pump stations, terminals and field offices, and whoever controls the orchestrator controls the configuration of every edge it manages. No oil and gas victim has been named for either flaw.

items.title: A second Check Point management-server flaw was a zero-day for two months — attacked in July, fixed and added to KEV on 22 September
items.content_text: Check Point disclosed CVE-2026-93616 on 22 September; neither the vendor nor CISA has published a CVSS score. It is a pre-authentication path traversal in the Security Management web service that lets a remote attacker run scripts and load Java classes on the server. Check Point says it saw a “handful of pinpointed attacks on July 23, 2026”, so the flaw was exploited about two months before a fix shipped on 22 September. Reporting lists Security Management Server, Multi-Domain Security Management, Log Server, Multi-Domain Log Server and SmartEvent as affected; advisory sk1000171 lists the fixed builds. CISA added it to KEV on 22 September with a federal deadline of 25 September. No actor or victim has been named. This is not CVE-2026-91843, the over-long-username flaw fixed on 17 September, which remains unexploited. The management server writes policy for every gateway it controls, including those at the IT/OT boundary of refineries, gas plants and pipeline control centres. A compromise dating back to July would not be removed by the 22 September fix.

items.title: One unauthenticated packet can crash TDengine, the time-series database some operators use behind telemetry and SCADA data — CVSS 7.5, fixed in 3.4.1.6, not exploited
items.content_text: Ridge Security disclosed CVE-2026-42542 on 23 September, a pre-authentication flaw in the RPC service of the open-source TDengine time-series database, which listens on TCP port 6030 by default. The vendor’s GitHub advisory, GHSA-vg95-j2hf-hvjx, describes an integer underflow in the uvConnMayGetUserInfo() function: a client-supplied message length is not validated, the calculation wraps around, and the resulting oversized memory copy crashes the taosd server process. No credentials or session are needed; a single crafted packet is enough. It is rated CVSS 7.5 (High), availability impact only. Affected are TDengine 3.4.0.0 through 3.4.1.5; the fix is 3.4.1.6. Ridge confirms remote denial of service, says plainly that it is not claiming code execution, and reports no telemetry of in-the-wild exploitation and no known public exploit code. Ridge names industrial telemetry, energy, utilities and factory-floor SCADA among the settings where TDengine runs. Its place on this page is editorial assessment: where a time-series store sits behind production, pipeline or compression telemetry, losing it blinds trending, alarm analytics and reporting even though control keeps running.

items.title: A hard-coded key and MD5 password hashes inside AVEVA Pipeline Integrity Monitor — read access to the project files is enough
items.content_text: CISA published advisory ICSA-26-253-01 on 10 September covering four vulnerabilities in the PIMBoards component of AVEVA Pipeline Integrity Monitor, AVEVA’s real-time leak-detection and integrity product for liquid and gas pipelines. All versions up to and including 2025 SP1 P1 are affected. CVE-2026-81821, a hard-coded cryptographic key (CVSS v3 8.4), lets anyone who can read PIMBoards project files decrypt the sensitive information inside them. CVE-2026-81822, weak MD5 password hashing (CVSS v3 8.4), exposes password hashes to brute force and a potential route to administrator access. CVE-2026-81823, missing authorisation (5.3), allows unauthorised reads of PIMBoards data, and CVE-2026-81824, a cross-site scripting flaw (4.7), lets a malicious link run script in a user’s session. AVEVA found the first two itself; researcher Adham Khairy Ramadan reported the others. The fix is the 2025 SP1 P2 security update, and AVEVA notes that migrating legacy project files to the new cryptography is one-way. No exploitation has been reported. This is the most directly pipeline-specific advisory of the period: whoever can read or administer PIM can see, and potentially change, the leak-detection configuration and dashboards that controllers rely on for safety decisions.

items.title: Schneider fixes a CVSS v4.0 9.2 authentication flaw in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety — and SCADAPack RTUs are in the same release
items.content_text: Schneider Electric’s September Patch Tuesday release on 8 September included SEVD-2026-251-04 for CVE-2026-3869, an incorrect implementation of an authentication algorithm (CWE-303) scored CVSS v4.0 9.2 (CVSS v3.1 9.8). The weakness is exposed when a project built at a lower application level runs, and can affect confidentiality, integrity and availability. Affected are Modicon M580 at application levels below 4.00 and Modicon M580 Safety below 4.20. Blastwave’s analysis does not list Modicon MC80 for this flaw; it notes that updated advisories in the same release add MC80, so check MC80 against those notices separately. The same release fixed a medium-severity defect in SCADAPack x70 RTUs and a high-severity issue in PowerLogic T300, and updated four existing advisories. Nothing in the release is reported as exploited. The sector relevance is our assessment rather than the vendor’s: M580 and M580 Safety controllers run process and safety functions in gas processing, terminals and refinery units, and SCADAPack RTUs are a common choice for wellsite automation and pipeline telemetry. An authentication weakness in a safety-rated controller is the kind of finding that belongs in the SIS change process, not the general patch queue.

items.title: A cluster with Sandworm-overlapping tooling and a Qilin ransomware affiliate got into Cisco firewall management consoles — the consoles that set your IT/OT boundary rules
items.content_text: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild. It is a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass: a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the appliance. CISA added it to KEV the same day with a federal remediation deadline of 12 September, now passed. Cisco Talos describes three post-compromise clusters. UAT-12197 used CVE-2026-20079 and is not attributed to a named actor. UAT-11823, an APT whose tooling overlaps with the Russian group Sandworm, used CVE-2026-20079 together with CVE-2026-20316 and deployed a variant of Cyclops Blink — Talos does not say Sandworm itself was responsible. UAT-11988, which Talos assesses with high confidence is a ransomware operator with TTPs consistent with Qilin affiliates, got in only through CVE-2026-20316, a CVSS 5.3 static-credential flaw that is not in KEV, and ultimately deployed Qilin. On 16 September Cisco published its hardening release, cisco-sa-hardening-asaftdfmc-uvpPROhN, covering eight internally found flaws across ASA, FTD and FMC (CVE-2026-20329 to CVE-2026-20336, maximum CVSS 9.9); it accompanies the exploited FMC flaws. No OT impact and no oil and gas victim has been named. But FMC is where the firewall policy between corporate networks and plant, pipeline SCADA and terminal control networks is written, so root on FMC is the ability to quietly loosen that boundary.

items.title: CISA adds five exploited flaws to KEV, including ScreenConnect — the remote-support tool that turns up on vendor-supplied OT PCs
items.content_text: CISA added the two MikroTik RouterOS flaws (CVE-2026-86060 and CVE-2026-67277) to the KEV catalog on 10 September, and the JFrog Artifactory and ConnectWise ScreenConnect flaws on 12 September, on evidence of active exploitation, with federal remediation deadlines of 13 September for RouterOS, 14 September for ScreenConnect and 25 September for Artifactory. Reporting indicates the Artifactory flaws were chained to gain administrator control, establish persistence and install Rust-based backdoors; ScreenConnect exploitation reportedly enabled unauthorised file transfer and execution through active sessions using a malicious VBScript payload; and the RouterOS entry reflects the CERT Polska chain covered separately on this page. No oil and gas victim is named. The ScreenConnect entry is the one to read twice: remote-support tools are how OEM service desks and integrators reach compressor-control panels, analyser shelters, terminal automation PCs and engineering workstations, and they are often installed by the vendor rather than by the operator’s own security team.

items.title: CISA adds Zyxel GS1900 switches to KEV after one actor pulled configs and root credentials from nearly a thousand of them — the switch class that turns up at small stations and contractor sites
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 21 September with a federal remediation deadline of 24 September. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel’s GS1900-series managed switches — GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2 — that lets an unauthenticated attacker with access to the management interface run operating-system commands through a crafted HTTP request. Zyxel patched it on 16 June in firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and the per-model equivalents, and gives no CVSS score, so we print none. GreyNoise’s report of the same day describes what it calls the first observed in-the-wild exploitation: a single actor, assessed by GreyNoise to be a Chinese speaker, compromised 996 GS1900 switches in 48 countries from on or about 17 August — Italy, the United States and Taiwan the largest shares — using an obfuscated Python tool that pulled device configurations and root-level password hashes over TFTP. GreyNoise says 564 of the victims were still on factory-default credentials. The same actor stole records from an unnamed western government organisation through two WordPress flaws and probed Gitea, UniFi, Proxmox and PAN-OS GlobalProtect; GreyNoise also assesses the actor as the same as, or related to, the group behind earlier Gitea exploitation, based on shared command-and-control infrastructure, malware and techniques — an assessment rather than an observation. No oil and gas victim is named and no OT impact is reported. The sector read is ours: GS1900 is an inexpensive managed switch, not industrial-rated, and it is exactly what a contractor or a small operator installs in a wellsite shelter, a meter station cabinet or a terminal office to hang cellular routers, cameras and an HMI PC off — the places where a device configuration in an attacker’s hands maps your remote-site network for them.

items.title: Check Point’s gateway VPN flaw is now being exploited and is in KEV — the Dutch NCSC’s “imminent” warning came true within days
items.content_text: On 22 September Check Point updated its advisory for CVE-2026-85102: improper validation of certificate data during VPN negotiation that lets an unauthenticated attacker run code on Security Gateways and Spark firewalls. The company says that “starting September 12, 2026, we observed a wave of exploitation attempts against Spark customers.” It gives no customer count and no attribution. CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day, with a federal remediation deadline of 25 September. Check Point published certificate indicators from the attempts: subjects CN=vpn, CN=vpn-user or CN=vpnuser, with OU=users and O=global. Fixes have been available since 9 September under sk1000117. The Dutch NCSC warned on 12 September that exploitation of this flaw and its sibling, CVE-2026-85103, was imminent. Only CVE-2026-85102 is in KEV and named as exploited; no exploitation of CVE-2026-85103 has been reported. Check Point also disclosed on 22 September that a different flaw, in its management server, had been attacked since July (see the separate card). Gateways of this class often sit at the IT/OT boundary of refineries, gas plants and pipeline control centres, and Spark appliances turn up at small remote sites. They terminate the vendor and contractor tunnels into those networks.

items.title: Check Point fixes a CVSS 9.8 pre-authentication root flaw in the servers that write your firewall policy — no exploitation reported
items.content_text: Check Point has fixed CVE-2026-91843, rated CVSS 9.8, in its Security Management and Log Servers, under advisory sk1000155, as reported by The Hacker News on 17 September and in SecurityWeek’s round-up. A stack overflow in the login process, triggered by an overly long username in an unauthenticated request, can give a remote attacker code execution as root. The Hacker News reports that a Trusted Clients misconfiguration is a precondition; that detail could not be confirmed in the vendor text, so check sk1000155 against your own configuration rather than relying on it. Reported affected versions are R82.10 up to Jumbo Hotfix Take 44, R82 up to Take 126, all builds of R82.20, R81.20 up to Take 166, R81.10 up to Take 190, and the end-of-support R81 and R80.x lines; Multi-Domain Server is affected and Smart-1 Cloud is already fixed. The fix is a LivePatch delivered through sk1000155. Check Point says there is “no indication that this vulnerability has been exploited in the wild.” This is separate from the VPN flaws the Dutch NCSC warned about on 12 September, and from CVE-2026-93616, a different management-server flaw that Check Point disclosed on 22 September as exploited (see the separate card). The management server is where policy for the gateways at the IT/OT boundary of refineries, gas plants and pipeline control centres is written, so root on it is the ability to change that boundary everywhere at once.

items.title: Rockwell revises its lock-out recovery notice a fifth time, adding Micro820 and Micro850 — the small controllers at wellsites and pump skids that attackers have been setting passwords on
items.content_text: Rockwell Automation published revision 5.0 of security notice SD1790, “Important Hardening Guidance for Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley Controllers and Instructions for Restoring Access When the Password Is Unknown”, on 18 September. First issued on 30 July alongside an FBI public service announcement, the notice describes threat actors remotely altering the configuration of internet-exposed programmable logic controllers, changing their IP addresses and setting passwords where none existed, so that operators lose access to their own equipment. Revision 2.0 added MicroLogix 1100 recovery steps in July; revision 4.0 in August clarified that setting a password alone is not a sufficient mitigation; revision 5.0 extends the recovery instructions and hardening guidance to Micro820 and Micro850 controllers alongside MicroLogix 1100 and 1400. There is no CVE, because there is no vulnerability: the activity works through internet exposure and missing or default credentials. The recommended actions are to remove controllers from the public internet, use a VPN for any remote access that is genuinely needed, isolate controllers behind firewalls on a separate OT network, set strong passwords and keep offline backups, monitor logs, keep firmware current and leave controllers in RUN mode so configuration cannot be changed remotely. The FBI announcement concerned water and wastewater; the sector link here is our assessment. MicroLogix and Micro800 controllers are the same low-cost class found at wellsite separators and chemical-injection skids, saltwater-disposal pumps, small compressor packages and tank-battery automation, often installed by a packager with a cellular modem and never surveyed again. Rockwell published no new product vulnerability advisories between 10 and 22 September.

items.title: A CVSS 10 authentication bypass in Cisco ISE is being exploited — the policy engine that decides who gets onto your network
items.content_text: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass in Cisco Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC. An API endpoint with insufficient authentication lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker bypass the web-based management interface. Cisco states that its PSIRT is aware of active exploitation, and all versions are affected until patched: 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4 carry the fix. There are no workarounds; Cisco points to infrastructure ACLs restricting management traffic as the only mitigation. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 16 September with a three-day federal deadline of 19 September, which has now passed. No new advisory revision has appeared; on 21 September Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency issued its own alert, AL-2026-126, urging the same patching, and ISE 3.0 is end-of-life and must be migrated rather than patched. No actor has been named, no indicators beyond checking access logs for unfamiliar usernames have been published, and no critical-infrastructure targeting has been claimed. The sector relevance is our assessment: ISE is the NAC and 802.1X policy engine that, in many operators, decides which devices and which vendor sessions are allowed onto the industrial DMZ and the plant network. Administrative control of it is administrative control of your segmentation policy.

items.title: A crafted email is enough: Cisco Secure Email Gateway SQL injection exploited as a zero-day, root without user interaction
items.content_text: Cisco advisory cisco-sa-esa-inj-2bLVGmhX, first published 14 September, covers CVE-2026-76461, a CVSS 9.8 SQL-injection flaw in AsyncOS email parsing on Cisco Secure Email Gateway. An unauthenticated attacker who sends a specially crafted email can run arbitrary SQL and then commands as root, with no user interaction and regardless of appliance configuration; physical and virtual appliances are both affected. Cisco says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in September 2026. Fixed builds are available, with 16.5.0-780 the preferred target and separate fixed builds for the 16.0 and 15.5 trains — outlets have printed inconsistent build strings, so take yours from the Cisco advisory. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 14 September with a federal deadline of 17 September, now passed. Shadowserver counted more than 400 exposed appliances. No attribution has been published and no industrial targeting has been reported. This is an IT mail gateway, not an OT device, and we list it for one reason: it is an unauthenticated, no-click path to root inside the enterprise that hosts your engineering workstations, historians and remote-access brokers.

items.title: mySCADA myPRO Manager hands privileged management functions to anyone who can reach it — CVSS 9.8, fixed in 2.2
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-258-03, published 15 September, covers two flaws in mySCADA myPRO Manager. CVE-2026-73807, CVSS v3 9.8, is a missing-authorisation flaw in the command API: an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the interface gets privileged management functions. CVE-2026-82567, CVSS 6.3 and adjacent-network only, allows unauthenticated sending of arbitrary SMS messages through a connected GSM modem. Versions up to and including 2.1 are affected; 2.2 is the fix. CISA lists Energy among the affected sectors, alongside Water and Wastewater, Critical Manufacturing, Food and Agriculture and Transportation, and states that no public exploitation targeting these flaws has been reported to it. The sector read is ours: myPRO is an inexpensive HMI and SCADA package that turns up at small and unmanned sites — gathering systems, small gas plants, tank farms and contractor-supplied skids — typically behind a cellular router with SMS alerting attached. Those are exactly the deployments least likely to appear in a corporate asset register.

items.title: CISA republishes the SCADAPack x70 credential flaw — the RTU family at wellheads, metering runs and compressor stations
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-258-04, published 15 September, republishes Schneider Electric’s 8 September notice SEVD-2026-251-03 and gives the flaw an identifier: CVE-2026-81861, CVSS v3 6.5 (v4 5.9), insufficiently protected credentials in the Secure Lock function. The consequence is unauthorised access to RTU configuration. The advisory lists SCADAPack 47x, 47xi, 47xd, 470R and 57x, with the product tree also naming SCADAPack 3xx and 32; CISA records the affected sectors as Critical Manufacturing and Energy. No code fix is listed in CISA’s machine-readable advisory — the remedies are configuration: enable role-based access control as set out in Schneider’s SCADAPack security guidelines, segment the RTU networks, and use the RTU Firewall Service to restrict which services are reachable. No exploitation has been reported. This is the CVE detail behind the SCADAPack line in Schneider’s September release, and it matters here more than the score suggests: these are the remote units that report and control at unmanned sites, often over cellular or licensed radio, where “who can read the configuration” is not a theoretical question.

items.title: About 20 flaws in one shared IO-Link master firmware base hit three vendors at once — unauthenticated root at the field layer
items.content_text: CERT@VDE published three advisories on 16 September that carry the same CVE range, CVE-2026-27546 through CVE-2026-27565, across three different brands: VDE-2026-014 for Pepperl+Fuchs ICE2-* and ICE3-* models, VDE-2026-027 for Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 EIP DI8 and IOL MA8 PN DI8, and VDE-2026-028 for Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 units. One shared CVE set across three vendors points to a common OEM firmware base. The worst two are CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass at CVSS 9.8, and CVE-2026-27565, an OS command injection at CVSS 9.8 reachable over the network without authentication or user interaction; below them sit command-injection and local-file-inclusion flaws at 8.8, an authorisation bypass at 8.1, path traversal at 7.5 and information disclosure at 6.5. The outcome is unauthenticated root code execution on the device and theft of stored password hashes and SSH private keys. Firmware below 1.7.4 is affected and the advisories name 1.7.8 as fixed — confirm the exact build with your vendor. On 24 September Nozomi Networks Labs published its technical write-up of the Pepperl+Fuchs findings (VDE-2026-014), counting 19 CVEs on the ICE2-8IOL-K45P-RJ45 it tested and showing that, chained, they give an unauthenticated attacker root on the device and the ability to manipulate sensor and actuator data. No exploitation has been reported. IO-Link masters aggregate sensors and actuators onto EtherNet/IP and PROFINET segments; in oil and gas they usually arrive inside packaged equipment — metering and analyser cabinets, custody-transfer skids, vendor process packages — rather than in the main DCS I/O count, which is why they are easy to miss.

items.title: CISA’s 22 September batch is led by a CVSS 9.8 code-execution flaw in the lwIP MQTT client — a library inside field devices, so the exposure has to come from each vendor
items.content_text: CISA published nine ICS advisories on 22 September, ICSA-26-265-01 through -09. The first two concern lwIP, the lightweight open-source TCP/IP stack embedded in many controllers, I/O modules, gateways and sensors. ICSA-26-265-01 covers the lwIP MQTT client application and CVE-2026-87121, CVSS v3.1 9.8 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N): an out-of-bounds write that “may allow an attacker to gain full code execution on the device.” ICSA-26-265-02 is a second advisory for lwIP itself. The other seven are six Siemens republications (Siveillance Control, SIPLUS and SIMATIC products, the Desigo CC family, Industrial Edge Management, SIMOVE Fleetmanager and SIPLANT, and WTV676/WTV776) and OpenPLC Runtime v3. No exploitation is reported and none of the batch is in KEV. The lwIP item is the one for oil and gas. The flaw sits in a library, not a product, so which RTUs, flow computers, gas detectors or wireless gateways are affected depends on whether their vendor built in lwIP’s MQTT client. That will only become clear as vendors publish their own notices. The Siemens items are mostly building-automation, physical-security and logistics products; check them against your estate using Siemens ProductCERT rather than the sector labels.

items.title: Seven new CISA ICS advisories plus one update on 17 September — Hitachi Energy FACTS, three Schneider products, Mitsubishi GX Works3, ABB Edgenius and an ELD
items.content_text: CISA released eight ICS advisories on Thursday 17 September — seven new, ICSA-26-260-01 through -07, plus one update: Bransys ELD, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, Hitachi Energy FACTS Control Platform, Schneider Electric Modicon M340 controllers and communication modules, Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 (750 and 755), ABB Ability Edgenius, and Schneider Electric PowerChute Serial Shutdown. GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings carry CVE-2026-15688, an authentication algorithm flaw scored CVSS v3.1 8.8 and v4.0 8.7, affecting all versions and enabling local authentication bypass and tampering with control programs. The Bransys electronic logging device has three hardcoded or cleartext credential flaws — CVE-2026-86520 (7.5), CVE-2026-86689 (5.9) and CVE-2026-77960 (5.3) — fixed in Android 11.00.00 and iOS 1.1.54. CISA’s machine-readable files now confirm four more. Modicon M340 and its X80 Ethernet modules (-04) carry CVE-2025-6625, a crafted-FTP-command denial of service scored CVSS v3.1 7.5 and v4.0 8.7, fixed from M340 firmware SV3.70 (with BMXNOE0100 3.60, BMXNOE0110 6.80 and BMXNOR0200H SV1.7_IR27 for the modules); it republishes a Schneider advisory first issued in August 2025, so the CVE year is not a typo. NetBotz 5, PowerChute and Edgenius are likewise republications of vendor advisories originally dated 11 August and 25 June. NetBotz 5 (-05) has an OS command injection, CVE-2026-13336 (v3.1 6.4, v4.0 7.3), plus CVE-2026-13337, fixed in 5.6.0. ABB Ability Edgenius (-06) inherits the Linux kernel “Copy Fail” privilege escalation, CVE-2026-31431 (7.8), fixed in 3.2.4.1. PowerChute Serial Shutdown (-07) has CVE-2026-13348, weak limits on authentication attempts (v3.1 5.3, v4.0 6.9), with version 1.6 as Schneider’s remediation. The Hitachi Energy advisory (-03) is not yet in the mirror; per reporting on Hitachi Energy advisory 8DBD000229, it covers CVE-2024-4872 and CVE-2024-3980 (CVSS 9.9), CVE-2024-3982 (8.2), CVE-2024-7940 (8.3, a service exposed without authentication) and CVE-2024-7941 (4.3) in FACTS Control Platform 3.4.0 to 4.1.1 where the GWS component is installed — see that advisory for remediation. CISA also updated ICSA-26-211-07, the Mitsubishi CC-Link IE TSN advisory, on 17 September, adding eight affected products. No exploitation is reported for anything in the batch, and none of its CVEs are in KEV; CISA’s KEV additions in the period were three Linux kernel flaws on 18 September (federal deadline 21 September, passed) and a Zyxel GS1900 switch flaw on 21 September, covered separately. The 22 September batch is covered separately. The two worth an oil and gas look are Modicon M340, a controller family common in utilities and balance-of-plant duties, and Edgenius, an industrial edge platform — judge both against your own estate rather than the sector labels.

items.title: ABB Freelance DCS controllers can be stopped by one crafted, unauthenticated network message — the fixes are already in shipped update rollups
items.content_text: ABB published advisory 7PAA010706 on 18 September for CVE-2023-5778, a missing length check in its Freelance distributed control system. An attacker with network access to an affected controller can send a specially crafted message that makes it stop; no credentials are needed. ABB scores it CVSS v3.1 7.5 (availability impact only). Affected are Freelance DCP, AC 700F, AC 800F and AC 900F controllers on Freelance 2013 and earlier, 2013 SP1, 2016, 2016 SP1, 2019 and 2019 SP1. The fixes already exist in Freelance 2013 SP1 RU06, 2016 SP1 RU07, 2019 SP1 RU03 and later rollups, 2019 SP1 FP1, and Freelance 2024, which is not affected. For AC 700F and AC 900F on Freelance 2016 and later, turning on Download-Protection from the Display Unit blocks the attack. ABB says the flaw had not been publicly disclosed or exploited when it issued the advisory. The sector link is our assessment, not ABB’s: Freelance runs process control in gas processing, compression, tank farms and smaller process plants, and many of those sites stay on older releases that never took the later rollups.

items.title: Moxa TN-4500B switches can be knocked over by an over-long username at the web login — CVSS 8.8, fixed in firmware 2.1
items.content_text: Moxa published advisory MPSA-252620 on 18 September for CVE-2026-15579 in its TN-4500B series Ethernet switches. Improper validation of the username field at web login lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker send an excessively long value that overflows a buffer and crashes the authentication process, producing a denial of service; Moxa scores it CVSS v4.0 8.8 with a network attack vector, no privileges and no user interaction, with high impact on availability and low impact on integrity. Firmware 2.0 and earlier is affected and 2.1 or later is the fix. Moxa credits researcher Mask Lu and reports no exploitation. Where an immediate update is not possible, Moxa’s mitigations are the usual ones: firewall the management interface, segregate operational networks with VLANs, disable unused services, use multi-factor authentication and strong passwords, and enable logging and monitoring. Be honest about fit before you act: the TN series is Moxa’s rolling-stock and vehicle-rated switch line, built for railway use, so it appears in oil and gas only where someone specified a vehicle-grade, wide-temperature switch — mobile or skid-mounted units and some offshore or vibration-heavy installations. If your register has none, the useful residue is the pattern: a management-plane crash on a switch that carries control traffic is an availability event for whatever sits behind it, so the reachability of switch web logins from anything other than a named engineering segment is worth confirming across your whole switch estate, Moxa or not.

items.title: The OT Cybersecurity Coalition asks CISA for a binding directive on federal agencies’ own OT — a proposal, not a CISA action, built on GAO’s finding that only 7 of 22 agencies met the device-inventory rules
items.content_text: CyberScoop reported on 6 October that the OT Cybersecurity Coalition has published a paper urging CISA to issue a Binding Operational Directive focused solely on operational technology at federal civilian agencies. The coalition wants the directive to assign responsibility at each agency, including an accountable OT cybersecurity officer, set minimum practices drawn from existing federal guidance, align with CISA’s 2022 Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals, and consider whether NSA’s OT guidance should apply to civilian agencies. In its words, “it is time for an encompassing BOD solely focused on OT security.” Earlier directives touched OT without being built for it. CISA did not respond to CyberScoop and has announced no directive. The paper leans on GAO-26-108937, published on 30 September: of 22 civilian CFO Act agencies reviewed, 15 had established inventories of networked IoT and OT devices, 11 maintained them, 10 included all required information, and only 7 met all three OMB requirements. GAO’s one recommendation is that OMB issue updated guidance covering these devices and oversee implementation. A directive would bind federal agencies only; the coalition’s argument is that it would also signal to the private sector what the government expects. For oil and gas operators the practical value today is GAO’s three tests, which work as a self-check on your own OT asset inventory.

items.title: GAO: industry panelists, energy among them, say overlapping federal cyber rules are hard to satisfy while fighting an incident — and the CIRCIA final rule is still not out
items.content_text: The Government Accountability Office published GAO-26-109197, “Cybersecurity Regulations: Industry Panelists Identify Duplication and Conflicts and Ways to Address Them”, on 28 September. It records a virtual panel held on 16 July with six industry representatives from the energy, financial services, and healthcare and public health sectors. Panelists said it could be difficult to meet every reporting requirement while also remediating a cyber threat, saw DHS and SEC rules as duplicating sector-specific ones, and half of them agreed that progress on harmonisation has been limited. Their suggestions were consistent timeframes, thresholds and definitions; a lead agency, such as CISA, to coordinate reporting; and more collaboration between government and industry. The report makes no formal GAO recommendations. It adds to a count already in circulation: on 8 September the McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce, drawing on GAO work, tallied 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. The rule most likely to change the picture has not arrived. No CIRCIA final rule had appeared in the Federal Register as of 6 October, so the September target in the regulatory agenda has passed; once in force, covered incidents are to be reported within 72 hours and ransom payments within 24. Oil and gas operators will recognise the problem: one event can trigger TSA pipeline security directive reporting to CISA, Coast Guard reporting for regulated terminals, SEC disclosure, state regulators, insurers and contractual notices.

items.title: CISA’s “Securing the Next 250” campaign: reduce attack surfaces, replace end-of-support devices, recover quickly — voluntary, but the end-of-support message lands on the field edge
items.content_text: CISA has launched “Securing the Next 250” for Cybersecurity Awareness Month, as reported by Industrial Cyber on 2 October. It is built around three Rs: Reduce attack surfaces, Replace end-of-support devices, and Recover quickly to sustain operations. Acting Director Nick Andersen framed it around dependency: when critical infrastructure is disrupted, “so are the businesses and communities that depend on vital services.” Beyond the three Rs the campaign promotes logging, backing up and encrypting data, reporting incidents to CISA, and keeping an incident response plan that is exercised, with realistic drills that include leadership and legal counsel at least once a year, and it singles out replacing end-of-support edge devices. It is guidance and promotion, not a requirement. The fit for oil and gas is editorial but direct: this edition’s exploited edge flaws — MikroTik routers, Citrix gateways, Cisco SD-WAN and FortiMail — are the class of device the Replace message is aimed at, and remote sites are where routers, gateways and switches tend to outlive their vendor support.

items.title: Texas Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian cites the tanker boardings and urges operators to “invest, test, monitor and strengthen” cyber defences — a statement, not a new rule
items.content_text: On 24 September the Railroad Commission of Texas issued a press release quoting Commissioner Wayne Christian, urging the state’s energy industry to prepare for evolving cyber threats. It is a commissioner’s statement, not a formal advisory or notice to operators, and it sets no new requirement and gives no technical guidance. It cites the August Coast Guard and FBI boarding of two foreign-flagged energy vessels bound for US ports, naming VL Prosperity, the crude tanker bound for Galveston (see the top story), and separate federal warnings that China-linked and Iran-affiliated cyber actors are targeting US critical infrastructure, including internet-connected operational technology and industrial control systems. It says it follows a notice the Commission sent to regulated operators earlier this year. Christian is quoted: “Texas is the energy capital of the world, and that makes our energy infrastructure a prime target for foreign adversaries,” and “We must invest, test, monitor and strengthen our defenses now.” He also calls for using AI to defend critical infrastructure. The statement reports no incident at any Texas operator and does not mention the Vivit Africa LNG carrier. For Texas producers, pipelines, processors and terminals, the practical read is that the state’s oil and gas regulator is publicly linking the maritime cargo compromises to operator readiness.

items.title: CISA and FBI put a number on integrator risk: one compromised automation vendor, nine archives, roughly 800 files of customers’ SCADA information and schematics
items.content_text: CISA and the FBI released a joint fact sheet, dated 23 September and publicised on 24 September, “Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working With Third-Party ICS Integrators”. It is built on a case from March and April 2025, when foreign cyber actors compromised the network of a US industrial automation company that provided system integration, engineering consulting and SCADA programming to industrial customers, including power utilities and transportation entities. Once inside, the actors searched for terms including “customers” and “SCADA” and staged roughly 800 files — customer SCADA information, ICS device details and schematics — in nine compressed archives for exfiltration. The fact sheet does not name the integrator, its customers or the actor, and describes no disruption. Its core advice is to limit every integrator connection to what a task requires and to replace continuous vendor connections with on-demand remote access that the operator enables, monitors and disables. No oil and gas customer is named; the relevance here is editorial assessment, because pipeline SCADA, compressor-station, wellsite-automation and terminal projects are routinely built and maintained by the same kind of integrator.

items.title: NIST opens comments on SP 800-82 Rev. 4, the OT security guide most programmes cite — rebuilt around CSF 2.0 and zero trust, with comments due 30 November
items.content_text: NIST released the initial public draft of SP 800-82 Revision 4, “Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security”, on 21 September, with comments due by 30 November 2026. NIST lists four main changes. The sector introduction expands to cover building automation, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels, and IIoT and cloud convergence. The guide is restructured around the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, and the old risk-management section is reorganised under the CSF Govern function. Guidance on implementing OT controls expands, including asset management and network monitoring and detection. The security architecture guidance now focuses on protecting system management functions and applying zero trust principles. Many oil and gas security programmes, internal standards and pipeline security reviews map to 800-82, so a revision changes the reference those documents point to. It is a draft, and nothing in it is binding until final. The comment period is the chance to say what does not work in a refinery or on a pipeline.

items.title: CISA’s cyber decoys guide: tripwires and honeytokens as detection you can add without touching production
items.content_text: CISA published “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. The guide defines decoys as assets that appear to be legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract adversaries, detect their presence or support intelligence collection, and it structures deployment in three phases: preparation, execution and analysis. CISA positions decoys alongside Zero Trust rather than as a replacement for either segmentation or monitoring. The reason it is worth an oil and gas reader’s time is the constraint it fits: most detection improvements in OT require touching a production system, and decoys mostly do not. A fake engineering workstation credential that no legitimate process uses, a planted project file, a dormant account named to look like a vendor login — each of these produces a signal with a very low false-positive rate and no change to the control system itself. That makes it one of the few detection moves that can be made between turnarounds rather than during one.
